blocks.text: 1. Perceptron
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444648951-557567341.png

Biological Neurons Versus Artificial Neurons, the previous topic, described a loose biological analogy, dendrites, a cell body, and firing. The Perceptron formalizes that analogy into precise, well-defined mathematics for the first time.

It is the first working, trainable model of an artificial neuron, introduced in the 1950s, directly connecting to the Perceptron's own history already covered in the History of Deep Learning topic, where its exciting early results and eventual, genuine limitation both got covered in depth.
2. The Perceptron's Mathematics

A Perceptron takes a vector of numeric inputs, x1 through xn, and a corresponding vector of weights, w1 through wn, one learned weight per input. It computes a weighted sum, multiplying each input by its own weight, adding all those products together, then adding a learned bias term.

A step function then converts this weighted sum into the Perceptron's final output: output 1 if the weighted sum exceeds a defined threshold, otherwise output 0. This entire mechanism, weighted sum plus a hard step function, is genuinely the mathematical core of the Perceptron model.

blocks.text: 3. The Step Function's Decision Rule
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444648952-941707015.png

The Perceptron's step function implements a genuinely simple decision rule. When the weighted sum lands above the defined threshold, the Perceptron outputs exactly 1, and when the weighted sum lands at or below that threshold, it outputs exactly 0.

There is no in-between value, no partial or uncertain output, the step function makes a hard, binary decision every single time. This simplicity is precisely what made the Perceptron easy to reason about mathematically, but it is also directly connected to the limitation covered later in this topic.
4. Linear Separability
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444648952-762556045.png

This connects directly back to the linearly separable limitation already covered in the History of Deep Learning topic. A Perceptron draws exactly one straight decision boundary, a single line in two dimensions, or a flat plane in higher dimensions.

It can only correctly separate data that a single straight line, or plane, can actually divide cleanly into its two output categories. Any dataset whose true separation requires a curved, or more complex, boundary is genuinely beyond what a single Perceptron can ever learn to solve correctly.
5. The Perceptron Learning Rule
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444649279-536279885.png

The Perceptron Learning Rule defines how its weights actually get adjusted during training. The Perceptron makes a prediction for a given training example, then compares that prediction directly against the actual, known correct answer for that example.

If the prediction was wrong, each weight gets nudged slightly in the direction that would have reduced that specific error. This process repeats across every training example, over multiple passes through the data, gradually shaping the Perceptron's weights toward a correct decision boundary, whenever one genuinely exists for the data at hand.
6. A Genuine Mathematical Guarantee

A genuine mathematical result called the Perceptron Convergence Theorem states that if the training data genuinely is linearly separable, the Perceptron Learning Rule is guaranteed to eventually find a perfectly separating line, given enough training passes.

If the data is not linearly separable, though, the algorithm will never converge at all, it keeps adjusting weights forever without ever actually succeeding, since no straight line exists that could satisfy every single training example simultaneously. This theorem is both a genuine strength and a direct preview of the limitation covered next.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This convergence guarantee is a genuinely elegant mathematical result for its time, one of the earliest formal proofs in the entire field of what would eventually become Deep Learning.

blocks.text: 7. The XOR Failure
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444649280-697301385.png

The XOR problem asks for an output of 1 only when exactly one of two binary inputs is 1, not when both are 0 and not when both are 1. This problem is genuinely not linearly separable, no single straight line can divide its four possible input combinations correctly.

A single Perceptron mathematically cannot solve XOR, regardless of how long it trains or how its weights get adjusted, a direct, provable consequence of the linear separability limitation covered earlier in this topic. This specific, formally proven failure directly caused the first AI winter, already covered in the History of Deep Learning topic.

blocks.text: 8. Why the Perceptron Still Matters
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444649281-210913546.png

The Perceptron still matters, despite this real, genuine limitation, because it is the exact mathematical foundation every larger neural network is ultimately built from. A single neuron inside a modern, large network computes essentially this same weighted sum, plus a bias, at its core.

Its specific limitation also directly motivated the very next topic in this module: Multi-Layer Perceptron, which stacks many Perceptron-like units together specifically to overcome this exact weakness, a direct, historically motivated response to the XOR failure covered in the previous section.
9. Modern Relevance
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444649281-294417000.png

A modern artificial neuron is genuinely a direct descendant of the Perceptron, sharing the exact same weighted sum plus bias structure covered throughout this topic. The core computation has not fundamentally changed since the 1950s.

The key upgrade that made modern neural networks so much more capable is replacing the Perceptron's hard step function with a smooth activation function instead, covered in full depth in the Activation Functions module immediately following this one, a change that turns out to matter enormously for what a network of these units can actually learn.
10. Worked Example
The example below implements a Perceptron from scratch, training it on a linearly separable problem, then demonstrating its failure on XOR.

code.content:
import numpy as np

def step_function(x):
    return 1 if x > 0 else 0

def train_perceptron(X, y, learning_rate=0.1, epochs=20):
    weights = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    bias = 0.0
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        for xi, yi in zip(X, y):
            prediction = step_function(np.dot(xi, weights) + bias)
            error = yi - prediction
            weights += learning_rate * error * xi
            bias += learning_rate * error
    return weights, bias

# Linearly separable problem: AND logic
X_and = np.array([[0, 0], [0, 1], [1, 0], [1, 1]])
y_and = np.array([0, 0, 0, 1])
weights_and, bias_and = train_perceptron(X_and, y_and)
and_predictions = [step_function(np.dot(x, weights_and) + bias_and) for x in X_and]
print(f"AND problem (linearly separable): predictions = {and_predictions}, actual = {list(y_and)}")

# NOT linearly separable: XOR logic
X_xor = np.array([[0, 0], [0, 1], [1, 0], [1, 1]])
y_xor = np.array([0, 1, 1, 0])
weights_xor, bias_xor = train_perceptron(X_xor, y_xor, epochs=100)
xor_predictions = [step_function(np.dot(x, weights_xor) + bias_xor) for x in X_xor]
print(f"XOR problem (NOT linearly separable): predictions = {xor_predictions}, actual = {list(y_xor)}")
print("\nNotice the AND problem solves perfectly, while XOR fails, exactly the limitation covered in this topic")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example directly demonstrates both halves of this topic: the Perceptron Learning Rule succeeding on a linearly separable problem, and failing, no matter how many epochs it trains, on the classic XOR problem.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: The Perceptron formalizes the biological neuron analogy into precise, well-defined mathematics.
It computes a weighted sum of inputs plus a bias, then applies a step function for a binary 0 or 1 output.
A Perceptron can only correctly separate data that a single straight line or plane can actually divide.
The Perceptron Learning Rule predicts, compares to the true answer, and nudges weights to reduce error, repeated across training.
The Perceptron Convergence Theorem guarantees success on linearly separable data, but guarantees failure to converge otherwise.
The XOR problem is not linearly separable, a formally proven failure that directly caused the first AI winter.
The Perceptron remains the mathematical foundation every larger network is built from.
A modern neuron shares the Perceptron's core structure, upgraded with a smooth activation function instead of a hard step.
Next up: Multi-Layer Perceptron, stacking many units together specifically to overcome the linear separability limitation.
